p: The Greek manuscripts read 'your wives'; Lake restores 'our', and the Plain English Translation follows him.

readings.w: Lake's text (his correction of the manuscripts)
The Greek manuscripts (G), as Lake's footnote reports

why: Polycarp is speaking in the first person plural ('let us teach ourselves', 4:1; 'let us teach our wives'), so 'our' fits the sentence. Lake's footnote: 'The MSS read ὑμῶν "your," but the confusion between ὑμῶν and ἡμῶν is so common that "our" may safely be restored.' In later Greek the two words were pronounced alike.
b: With 'your', Polycarp would be telling the Philippian men to teach their own wives. Either way the teaching is the same.

t: Did Eusebius have 'the word of righteousness'?
p: Eusebius's quotation of this verse lacks 'the word of righteousness'.

readings.w: The Greek manuscripts (G) and the Latin (L), Lake's text
readings.en: to obey the word of righteousness

why: Two independent witnesses, the Greek manuscripts and the Latin, have the phrase, and Lake prints it. Eusebius may have shortened, or his copy lacked the words. Lake's footnote: 'τῷ λόγῳ τῆς δικαιοσύνης GL, om. Eus.'
b: The NPNF English of Eusebius reads 'to be obedient and to practice all patience'. Hebrews 5:13 has the same Greek phrase, which the site renders 'the message of righteousness'.

p: Most Latin manuscripts have no 'and' between the two words; two have it. English needs the 'and' either way.

readings.w: Lake's text (most manuscripts of the Latin)
Two manuscripts of the Latin, as Lake's footnote reports

why: Lake prints the text without 'et'. His footnote: 'An et after casti would be natural, but it is only found in two of the MSS of L.' The meaning does not change; English joins the two words with 'and' in both cases.

a: you who are at the beginning of his letter
t: 'At the beginning of his letter' or 'his letters in the beginning'?
p: The Greek is lost here. Lake guesses that it said the Philippians 'were his epistles in the beginning', and Lightfoot's English follows the guess.

readings.orig: qui estis in principio epistulae eius
readings.en: who are in the beginning of his letter
readings.plain: you who are at the beginning of his letter

readings.w: Lake's footnote: a guess at the lost Greek, which Lightfoot's English follows
readings.orig: τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐπιστολαῖς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: who were his epistles in the beginning
readings.plain: who were his letters in the beginning

why: The Latin is the only witness, and Lake prints it. His footnote: 'The Greek was perhaps τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐπιστολαῖς αὐτοῦ, and ought to be rendered "who were his epistles in the beginning," with a reference to II Cor. 3, 2.' That is a reconstruction, not a reading found in any manuscript, so the Plain English Translation keeps the Latin. Lake's own English follows the Latin too: 'who are praised in the beginning of his Epistle'.
b: With the guess, Polycarp would be echoing 2 Corinthians 3:2, "You yourselves are our letter", and calling the Philippians Paul's living letters. With the Latin, he points to Paul's warm opening words to them (Philippians 1:3-11). See the note at 11:3.

p: Some Latin manuscripts read 'God' for 'the Lord'.

readings.en: which alone then had known the Lord

readings.w: Some manuscripts of the Latin, as Lake's footnote reports
readings.en: which alone then had known God

why: Lake prints dominum; his footnote: 'Some MSS. of L read deum instead of dominum.' Lightfoot's English, 'which alone at that time knew God', follows the other reading. The difference does not change the sense of the sentence.

p: Some Latin manuscripts leave out 'and God', so that the phrase is only 'our Lord Jesus Christ'.

readings.orig: in dominum nostrum et deum Iesum Christum
readings.en: in our Lord and God Jesus Christ

readings.w: Some manuscripts of the Latin, as Lake's footnote reports

why: Lake prints et deum; his footnote: 'Et deum is omitted by some of the MSS of L.' A scribe is more likely to have dropped the unusual title than to have added it, but it could also be an addition from John 20:28. The Greek is lost.
b: This variant matters for the history of how early writers spoke of Christ as God. Lightfoot's English has 'our Lord and God Jesus Christ'.

p: Eusebius has the present 'I send'; the Latin has a future, 'I will send'.

readings.w: The Latin (L): misero, which Lake's footnote says stands for πέμψω
readings.en: or one whom I will send

why: For chapter 13 the only Greek is Eusebius's quotation, and Lake prints it. The Latin's future (misero, Greek πέμψω) is one letter different in Greek. Lake's footnote: 'πέμπω Eus. misero (= πέμψω) L.' The sense is the same: Polycarp plans to send someone.
